subject_definitions
  References supplied with this generation:
    <Picture 1>  federphibium (char)
    <Picture 2>  der frosch (char)
    <Picture 3>  das huhn (char)
    <Picture 4>  board (style)
    <Picture 5>  der forscher (char)
    <Picture 6>  pond (loc)
    <Picture 7>  henhouse interior (loc)
    <Audio 1>    this window of the song

  REFERENCE - read this first
    Seven images are supplied. Four are subjects, one is the look, two are places.

    <Picture 1> THE FEDERPHIBIUM, the hybrid child: a fat green toad body with a
    red chicken comb, a red wattle under the chin, a small yellow-orange beak, huge
    orange-ringed eyes set high and wide, a pale cream belly, dark green speckling,
    frog legs with long toes ending in small yellow claws, and two small useless
    white-and-green feathered wings on its flanks.
    <Picture 2> DER FROSCH.  <Picture 3> DAS HUHN.
    <Picture 5> DER FORSCHER, seen from behind, which is how he is always seen.

    <Picture 4> is NOT a thing in the scene. It is a colour and construction board:
    the palette, the line weight, and the way a shadow is shaped. Read the look off
    it and never draw it.
    <Picture 6> is the pond, <Picture 7> the inside of the hen house. They are
    background paintings that set the colour and the architecture of those places.
    Neither is a character and nothing in them is a subject.

    Take from the character references: the design, the proportions, the colour
    model, the exact shape of comb, wattle, beak, eyes, wings and claws.
    Do NOT take their rendering. They carry soft painterly shading, and each figure
    stands on a plain grey backdrop with a cast shadow under it. This film is cel
    animation - flat fills, hard-edged shadow shapes, no gradients, no gloss.
    Redraw them in that idiom, and never reproduce the grey backdrop or that
    shadow. Never reproduce lettering, caption, logo, watermark or frame from any
    reference.

  CAST - the reference is the child, and the parents are it taken apart
    DER FROSCH - <Picture 2>. The narrator, and the only one who ever speaks. Green
    warty skin, dark speckling, a pale cream belly, huge orange-ringed eyes, long
    clawed toes, a potbellied sitting build, a wide frog mouth. He is what
    <Picture 1> is with every chicken part taken away: NO comb, NO wattle, NO beak,
    NO wings. Permanently wet, with a
    visible sheen. He wears nothing and owns nothing. Earnest, lovesick, entirely
    without shame.
    DAS HUHN - <Picture 3>. A plain brown farmyard hen carrying exactly the chicken parts that
    <Picture 1> borrowed: the same red comb, the same red wattle, the same
    yellow-orange beak, the same scaly legs and claws. Otherwise completely
    ordinary and completely oblivious. She never once deliberately looks at him -
    everything that reads as a response is coincidence, she was pecking anyway,
    she turned her head anyway. Beady black eyes. No eyelashes, no blush, no
    anthropomorphism of any kind.
    DIE FEDERPHIBIEN - the imagined children: <Picture 1> exactly, in numbers.
    Comb, wattle, beak, frog body, stub wings, clawed webbed feet. The wings
    cannot lift them and they will not swim, and they do not know it yet. They
    appear ONLY inside the chorus fantasies, never in the real pond.
    DER FORSCHER - <Picture 5>. The only human being in the film, and the film never shows his
    face. Khaki trousers, a plain shirt with the sleeves turned back, a straw hat.
    A hardbound notebook and a pencil, and an SLR on a black strap round his neck -
    most of the time only the strap is visible, the body and lens of the camera
    only in the close shots of the notebook and at the very end when he finally
    uses it. Middle aged, unhurried, completely absorbed. He sits on a folding
    chair at the edge of the pond and draws what he sees, in the fine pencil manner
    of a nineteenth century scientific plate, the parts labelled in a small hand.
    Always seen from behind or over his shoulder. Never his face, never a reaction
    shot, never a word. He does not interact with the animals and they never notice
    him. He moves quickly exactly once, when he jumps up and grabs the chair to
    stop it going over.

  WORLD
    A murky farm pond at the bottom edge of a chicken yard. High summer, humid,
    overcast bright. Green scum water, cattails, duckweed. A leaning chicken-wire
    fence with a gap worn under it. A corrugated tin coop. Dry mud cracked into
    plates. One bare bulb on a sagging cable. Flies everywhere.
    The farm plainly works - the coop is repaired, there is feed on the ground -
    and nobody is home. The one person who ever appears is the researcher at the
    pond, and he is never shown from the front. Never explain either of those.

  RUNNING GAGS
    The frog is always wet. Wherever he sits a small dark puddle forms, and it is
    still there after he moves away.
    Flies orbit his head in every single beat. He never eats one. Not once.
    One single corn kernel keeps coming back - dropped, carried, offered, ignored.
    The hen never blinks at the same time as he does.
    Hearts appear exactly twice in the whole film and nowhere else: rising over the
    frog's head when the focus comes back to him, and circling the pair as they
    clear the hen house door. Both times they are flat hard-edged cartoon shapes,
    drawn like everything else, held a moment and gone. Never a constant, never
    throbbing, never a drifting background of them. Everywhere else the film
    refuses that shorthand.

  RULES
    Only the frog speaks, and only in the song's own words. Keep his lines in
    German exactly as written.
    The hen makes real chicken sounds and nothing else. She is never given a human
    reaction, never a take, never a double-take.
    The frog never looks into the lens until the final beat.
    Nothing here is cute. Everything is sincere. The sincerity is the joke - so
    never play it for laughs, never mug, never wink.

summary
  The farmyard lies still around its pond. In the water there is only a small dark shape at first, which resolves into a frog: he kicks his legs in slow swimming strokes and jerks forward with each push, the way a frog actually moves through water.

retention_analysis
  Hand-drawn 2D cel animation as made for television in the mid 1990s: ink and
  paint on acetate cels, photographed over painted backgrounds. Cheap, fast,
  slightly grubby work by people who could draw. Reproduce the CRAFT of that era,
  never the condition of an old tape.

  LINE
    Brush-and-ink outlines with real taper - the line swells and thins along its
    length and closes every shape. The line is not uniform and not confident:
    slight wobble, the odd overshoot at a corner, thickness varying between
    drawings of the same character. One line weight per character, scaled to the
    shot size, so a close-up is not just an enlargement.
    Self-coloured lines where it suits - a dark olive outline on a green animal, a
    deep umber on a brown one - with black kept for accents.

  COLOUR AND FILLS
    Flat fills. No gradients, no soft rendering, no ambient occlusion, no gloss.
    Shadows are a SEPARATE flat shape with a hard edge, one or two steps darker on
    the same hue - never a blur, never a multiply wash. Highlights are the same
    idea inverted.
    Palette dusty and slightly off: mustard, moss, liver brown, dishwater blue,
    a sour pink. Two or three saturated accents per shot at most. Each character
    has a fixed colour model that never drifts between shots.

  BACKGROUNDS
    Gouache or watercolour on board: visibly brushy, textured, unoutlined, edges
    softer than the characters. Warmer and duller than the figures so the cels pop
    off them. Real botany and real architecture - a specific fence, a specific
    weed - rather than generic cartoon shapes.
    The mismatch between crisp outlined characters and soft painted backgrounds IS
    the look. Lean into it rather than harmonising it.

  DIRT AND DETAIL
    Everything in the world is used. Chipped paint, rust bloom at a bolt, dried
    mud in the tread of a tyre, a scuffed floor, seed husks and hair on the
    ground, flies that are actually drawn. Wet things read wet, dry things read
    dusty.
    In close-ups the detail goes UP, not down: pores, chapped skin, a split claw,
    crumbs at the corner of a mouth. The wide shots stay simple and graphic.

  MOVEMENT
    Limited animation on twos, twelve drawings a second. Pose-to-pose with strong
    readable key poses and very few in-betweens. Held cels for long stretches.
    Cycled blinks and walks.
    Rubbery squash, stretch and deformation reserved for single accents, taken
    further than is comfortable, then straight back to a held pose.
    Smears drawn as a shape rather than rendered as motion blur. Dry-brush speed
    lines where something moves fast.
    Lipsync from a fixed mouth chart of about ten shapes, so the mouth SNAPS
    between positions rather than morphing. Expressions come from a small reused
    library. Eyes are simple ovals with dot or pinprick pupils.

  CAMERA
    Rostrum and multiplane thinking: lateral pans across a long background
    painting, truck-ins on a held cel, simple zooms, layered foreground elements
    for depth. No 3D camera, no arcing moves, no rack-focus theatrics.
    Composition centred and TV-safe.

  THE GROSS-UP
    Once per scene at most, on a punchline: cut to a single fully painted,
    high-detail, properly rendered illustration - wet skin, mucus, the grain of a
    scaly leg, a bead of water - which abandons the flat cel style entirely for
    one or two seconds, then cut straight back. This is a deliberate 1990s device.
    Render it CLEAN and sharp, like a painted plate, not like damaged footage.

  RENDER CLEAN - this matters
    Output a pristine, stable, sharp image. Do NOT add film grain, video noise,
    VHS softness, tape dropouts, tracking lines, head-switching noise, scanlines,
    interlace combing, chroma bleed, dot crawl, colour fringing, chromatic
    aberration, gate weave, registration wobble, frame jitter, dust, scratches,
    hair in the gate, vignetting, halation, bloom, letterbox bars, timecode or
    any on-screen text. No lens effects of any kind.
    Every one of those is being added afterwards in the grade, and baked-in
    artefacts cannot be removed. Full frame, clean edges, steady.

  Hold identical across every scene of this film: the colour model, the
  line weight, the proportions and the costume of every character named
  above, and the time of day and weather of the location.

detailed_description
  [Static shot] Close on the water surface where the dark shape moves.

  The farmyard lies still around its pond. In the water there is only a small dark shape at first, which resolves into a frog: he kicks his legs in slow swimming strokes and jerks forward with each push, the way a frog actually moves through water. He covers half the distance to the bank.

overall_soundscape
  Under everything, always present and always quiet: a summer farm pond. Wet
    plops, crickets, the low mutter of hens somewhere off frame, corrugated tin
    ticking in the heat, and one distant tractor that never arrives. Never louder
    than the vocal.
    NO cartoon sound effects. No boings, no slide whistles, no rubber-band twangs,
    no comedy impacts on cuts. The frog's quakes and the hen's clucks are the only
    animal sounds, and both are recorded-real rather than performed.
    The film never uses sound to tell you something is funny.

non_diegetic_music
  The provided song excerpt is the ONLY music. Do not invent, add or extend any
    instrumentation - no score, no stings, no risers.
